Chapter 4: The Limits of Tradition—When Old Answers No Longer Satisfy
As the conversation unfolded, you could almost feel the younger man's confidence slipping away. He’d walked into that courthouse feeling sure of himself—armed with the teachings and customs he’d grown up with. But every answer he gave was met with yet another question. The older man just kept chipping away, quietly and persistently.
If you’ve ever tried defending something you believe in, only to run into honest, searching doubt, you probably know exactly how he felt. At first, tradition feels rock-solid—those rituals, stories, all the rules—they bring order and meaning to your life. But when you really start to examine them, the cracks start to show. The stories don’t always line up. The rules can even conflict. And sometimes, the reasons behind it all? They’re kind of fuzzy.
The younger man tried to lean on what he’d always known. He talked about honoring the gods and following the examples set by his ancestors. But the older man wasn’t letting that slide. He pointed out something pretty sharp: even the gods, in the old stories, don’t always agree on what’s right. So, if tradition comes from the will of these gods, and the gods themselves can’t agree, how can tradition really be a reliable guide?
That realization is unsettling, isn’t it? It’s one thing to question a single rule or custom. But to start doubting the whole framework that gives your life meaning—that’s a whole different level. Suddenly, the younger man found himself in new, uncomfortable territory. He had to admit, he didn’t have all the answers. And the older man? He didn’t seem interested in “winning” the argument. He just wanted him to honestly reflect.
Most of us, when we hit the limits of tradition, get defensive or just deny it altogether. Letting go of beliefs that shaped your identity is tough. Admitting those beliefs might be wrong or incomplete? That’s even harder. But outside that courthouse, the conversation showed something important—this kind of self-examination isn’t just possible; it’s necessary.
The older man’s approach—asking questions, listening closely, refusing to settle for easy answers—showed a whole new way of thinking. It’s about valuing understanding over certainty. He proved it’s possible to respect tradition, while also seeing where it falls short. You can honor the past, without letting it hold you back.
Suddenly, the courthouse—once a symbol of authority and order—became the stage for a different kind of trial. This wasn’t about guilt or innocence, but about ideas, beliefs, and even the self. The outcome? Totally uncertain. But what really mattered was the process. It was transformative. And it made something clear: searching for truth isn’t about reaching some final destination. It’s a journey—one that calls for honesty, humility and, above all, the courage to face the unknown.
